Guided trip

Back to the Moon

Artemis: round the Moon again, and where they mean to land. Then back to Earth.

Open the trip: Back to the Moon

The last footprints

This valley is where people last stood on the Moon. In December 1972 two astronauts of Apollo 17, Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, drove away from here, climbed into their lander, and left. For more than fifty years after that, nobody travelled further from the Earth than a space station.

Four people leave again

Then four people left from this coast of Florida, on a flight called Artemis Two: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and, from Canada, Jeremy Hansen. They were the first crew to leave the Earth's neighbourhood since Apollo.

Round the far side

They did not land. Their ship swung once round the far side of the Moon, the side we never see from home, and at its farthest it was more than four hundred and six thousand kilometres from the Earth, further than Apollo 13. No people had ever been so far away.

Home, from out there

From out here the whole Earth is a small, bright ball in the dark. The flight lasted nine days and ended with a splashdown in the sea. It was a test of the ship and of the people, for what comes next.

Where they mean to land

This is the Moon's south pole. Some crater floors here never receive light from the Sun, and they have kept water ice for billions of years. Ice is water to drink, air to breathe and fuel for the journey home. This is the region the Artemis flights are meant to explore.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
